LaQX: A JAX Toolkit for Neural Quantum State Simulations of Lattice Quantum Many-Body Models

Yuntian Gu1,2⋆\star, Chaohui Fan1,3, Ruichen Li1, Haoxiang Chen1,4,
Weizhong Fu1,4, Yixiao Chen1, Dingshun Lv1, Weiluo Ren1,

Abstract

Neural quantum states provide accurate variational representations for interacting lattice fermions and spins. Turning a new ansatz into a reproducible calculation, however, requires coordinated implementations of the Hamiltonian, sampling, optimization, observables, and accelerator parallelism. We present LaQX (Lattice Quantum simulation based on jaX), an open-source neural quantum state library based on JAX that organizes these components through common functional interfaces. Beyond ground-state variational Monte Carlo, LaQX supports excited-state calculations, Green’s Function Monte Carlo refinement, adiabatic evolution, and real-time evolution with time-dependent variational Monte Carlo. It consolidates methods developed in recent high-accuracy neural quantum state studies of the Hubbard model and frustrated magnets [24, 23, 19], and the package has been used to investigate the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model [25]. We document these capabilities with reproducible calculations for Hubbard, J𝟏J_{1}-J𝟐J_{2} Heisenberg, altermagnetic Hubbard, and interacting Hofstadter models. Function-oriented modules separate the scientific components and limit the source context needed for extensions by human developers and large language models. Source code, documentation, and executable examples are available at https://github.com/bytedance/laqx.

1 Introduction

Lattice models connect microscopic Hamiltonians to collective quantum phenomena. Their numerical solution is nevertheless difficult because the Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially with system size. Exact diagonalization (ED) is consequently restricted to finite clusters [52], density-matrix renormalization group [66] and matrix product state (MPS) methods [56] are most effective in one dimension and quasi-one-dimensional geometries, and higher-dimensional tensor-network contractions require additional approximations [15, 67]. Quantum Monte Carlo [20, 52, 2, 4, 68] can reach much larger systems when a non-negative sampling weight is available, but frustration and fermionic statistics can produce a sign problem whose generic resolution is computationally hard [34, 63]. Comparisons on paradigmatic models such as the Hubbard model [29] therefore continue to rely on complementary numerical methods with different controlled limits [32, 42, 1].

Neural quantum states (NQS) add a flexible class of variational wavefunctions to this landscape. In variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [20, 4], a neural network represents the many-body amplitude, and its parameters are optimized using stochastic estimates over the Born distribution [9]. The field now encompasses a broad range of architectures and applications [31, 37]. Early work combined restricted Boltzmann machines with conventional fermionic pair-product states [39], while convolutional networks addressed frustrated magnets [14] and autoregressive recurrent networks enabled direct sampling [27]. Subsequent developments introduced symmetry-aware deep networks for frustrated spin systems [50], neural backflow and hidden-fermion constructions for lattice fermions [35, 47, 33], and variational protocols for excited states and dynamics [40, 54].

Recent studies have used hidden-fermion Pfaffian states [48], Transformer backflow [24, 65], convolutional backflow [23], and symmetry-preserving pairing states [45] to investigate the ground states of the square-lattice tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model. Large-scale NQS calculations have also examined topological superconductivity and quantum criticality in the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model [25, 49]. Combining neural networks with tensor networks provides another route to correlated variational states [19]. These studies compare energies and order-specific correlations across variational families to distinguish competing phases. The range of fermionic, spin, excited-state, and dynamical applications motivates software that can accommodate new methods without duplicating the full VMC workflow.

Reusable software has developed alongside these methods. NetKet and jVMC provide general NQS and VMC infrastructure [64, 55], while Quantax is a JAX package for flexible lattice many-body and NQS calculations [11]. In the complementary setting of first-quantized, real-space electronic structure, FermiNet established the accuracy of antisymmetric neural wavefunctions [41, 60], and JaQMC provides an open JAX framework for neural-network VMC and diffusion Monte Carlo [43, 7]. Together with recent GPU-vectorized tensor-network VMC [17], these efforts show that accelerator performance depends not only on the cost of a single wavefunction evaluation, but also on batched sampling, differentiation, and linear algebra. They also establish the value of independent codebases with different physical scope and extension patterns.

Built on JAX [5], LaQX targets interacting lattice fermions and spins. It provides neural backflow and tensor-network states, symmetry projection, Metropolis-Hastings sampling, first-order and natural-gradient optimization, and observable evaluation. The same interfaces support ground-state VMC with optional Green’s Function Monte Carlo (GFMC) [62, 58] refinement, joint optimization of low-lying states with Natural Excited States (NES) [40], measurements on trained states, adiabatic evolution by variational continuation, and real-time evolution with time-dependent VMC (tVMC).

LaQX consolidates the computational framework developed for neural quantum state calculations of the doped Hubbard model, including Transformer-backflow states and the MARCH optimizer [24], followed by the SCALE and ACE convolutional backflow architectures [23]. It also incorporates architecture that combine convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with MPS, denoted CNN-MPS, for frustrated magnets [19]. The convolutional-backflow and CNN-MPS studies report variational energies among the best available for their respective fermionic and spin benchmarks. LaQX has subsequently been applied to the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model, where NQS and independent projected entangled pair state (PEPS) calculations provided complementary real-space evidence of spin-charge separation [25]. The present release brings these developments together in a documented package that supports multiple ansatz families and physical workflows.

The implementation is deliberately function-oriented. Wavefunctions, physical operators, samplers, and parameter updates are connected through small interfaces, with numerical state passed explicitly between them. This separation makes JAX transformations directly applicable and allows many scientific extensions to remain local to one component. It also supports programming with large language models (LLMs), including the conversational workflow known as vibe coding [53]. Limiting cross-component dependencies reduces the source context needed for an extension. Section 3.2 illustrates these extension paths.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the numerical methods and notation. Section 3 describes the software architecture. Section 4 presents calculations for Hubbard, J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg, altermagnetic, and interacting Hofstadter models.

2.2 Neural wavefunction architectures

SCALE and ACE are convolutional neural backflow states for lattice fermions [23], while CNN-MPS combines convolutional features with a tensor-network output for spins [19]. Their feature extractors use the same elementary operations: occupation embeddings, spatial convolutions, and site-wise multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) [51]. We define these operations first, then specify how each architecture constructs the many-body amplitude.

Occupation embeddings and convolutional features.

Let Ns=Lx​LyN_{s}=L_{x}L_{y} denote the number of spatial sites, and let qiq_{i} label the local basis state at site ii. For spinful fermions, qi=ni↑+2​ni↓q_{i}=n_{i\uparrow}+2n_{i\downarrow} distinguishes the four states |0⟩|0\rangle, |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle, |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle, and |↑↓⟩|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle; for a spin-1/21/2 or spin-polarized occupation basis, qi∈{0,1}q_{i}\in\{0,1\}. SCALE and sparse updates.

2.3 Sampling and ground-state optimization

Metropolis-Hastings sampling.

A Markov chain samples configurations from p�p_{\theta} [38, 26]. LaQX constructs proposals from the off-diagonal terms of the Hamiltonian: an allowed hopping or spin-exchange term generates a candidate configuration 𝐧′\mathbf{n}^{\prime} from 𝐧\mathbf{n}. A proposal 𝐧′∼q⁡(𝐧′|𝐧)\mathbf{n}^{\prime}\sim q(\mathbf{n}^{\prime}|\mathbf{n}) is accepted with probability

a⁡(𝐧→𝐧′)=min⁡{1,|�(𝐧′)|2|�(𝐧)|2​q⁡(𝐧|𝐧′)q⁡(𝐧′|𝐧)}.a(\mathbf{n}\to\mathbf{n}^{\prime})=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{|{}_{\theta}(\mathbf{n}^{\prime})|^{2}}{|{}_{\theta}(\mathbf{n})|^{2}}\frac{q(\mathbf{n}|\mathbf{n}^{\prime})}{q(\mathbf{n}^{\prime}|\mathbf{n})}\right\}. (17)

Otherwise the chain remains at 𝐧\mathbf{n}. Including the forward-reverse proposal ratio accommodates asymmetric proposals while satisfying detailed balance with the Born distribution. Local occupation moves preserve the sampled particle-number or magnetization sector.

Stochastic reconfiguration.

LaQX provides Adam [30], SPRING [22], and MARCH [24]. Adam uses the energy-gradient covariance in Eq. (4) to construct adaptive first- and second-moment updates. The latter two methods are derived from stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [59]: instead of descending in the Euclidean geometry of the parameters, SR projects an imaginary-time step onto the tangent space of the variational state.

In the implementation, local energies are clipped before centering at the sample median plus or minus a chosen multiple of the mean absolute deviation from that median. Real and imaginary parts are clipped separately. Reported energies and energy variances per site use the unclipped local energies.

SPRING.

Subsampled Projected-Increment Natural Gradient Descent (SPRING) retains the preceding unscaled direction rather than selecting a minimum-norm solution independently for each batch [22]. Subscripts kk on XkX_{k} and eke_{k} denote the sample arrays at optimization step kk. Let dk−1d_{k-1} be the stored direction, �\mu the momentum decay coefficient, and mk=�​dk−1m_{k}=\mu d_{k-1} the decayed direction. SPRING obtains the new unscaled direction dkd_{k} by solving

dk=mk+Xk𝖳​(Xk​Xk𝖳+�​I+Rk)−1​(ek−Xk​mk).d_{k}=m_{k}+X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}+\lambda I+R_{k}\right)^{-1}(e_{k}-X_{k}m_{k}). (23)

The extra stabilizer is Rk=‖Tk‖F​�0R_{k}=\|T_{k}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\Pi_{0}, where Tk=Xk​Xk𝖳T_{k}=X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}} is the sample-space Gram matrix and ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}} is the Frobenius norm. For real states, �0=𝟏B​𝟏B𝖳/B\Pi_{0}=\mathbf{1}_{B}\mathbf{1}_{B}^{\mathsf{T}}/B projects onto the constant sample vector, with 𝟏B\mathbf{1}_{B} the length-BB vector of ones. For complex states it projects separately onto the constant vectors of the real and imaginary sample blocks. Centering gives Xk𝖳​�0=0X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}\Pi_{0}=0 and �0​ek=0\Pi_{0}e_{k}=0, so this term does not change the exact-arithmetic solution of Eq. (22); it stabilizes the numerical solve in these null directions.

The Moment-Adaptive ReConfiguration Heuristic (MARCH) extends this construction by weighting parameter directions according to a second-moment accumulator [24]. In the notation of Eq. (20), the minimization objective is

2.4 Natural Excited States

The natural excited states (NES) method turns the calculation of the lowest KK states into a ground-state variational problem on the tensor product of KK replicas of the physical Hilbert space [40]. Let 𝒩=(𝐧1,…,𝐧K)\mathcal{N}=(\mathbf{n}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{n}_{K}) contain one many-body configuration per replica. Given KK trainable state functions a, define the matrix with replica index bb labeling rows and state index aa labeling columns, where a,b=1,…,Ka,b=1,\ldots,K,

Mb​a(𝒩)=(𝐧b)a, (𝒩)=detM(𝒩).M_{ba}(\mathcal{N})={}_{a}(\mathbf{n}_{b}),\qquad\Psi(\mathcal{N})=\det M(\mathcal{N}). (29)

The expanded Hamiltonian is the Kronecker sum of KK copies of the physical Hamiltonian HH,

ℋ\displaystyle\mathcal{H} =⨁b=1KH=∑b=1KH(b),\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{b=1}^{K}H=\sum_{b=1}^{K}H^{(b)}, (30)
H(b)\displaystyle H^{(b)} =I⊗(b−1)⊗H⊗I⊗(K−b).\displaystyle=I^{\otimes(b-1)}\otimes H\otimes I^{\otimes(K-b)}.

Here ⨁\bigoplus denotes the Kronecker sum, ⊗\otimes the tensor product, and II the identity on one replica, with I⊗0=1I^{\otimes 0}=1. Thus H(b)H^{(b)} acts only on replica bb. The determinant makes \Psi antisymmetric under exchange of replicas. If E1≤E2≤⋯E_{1}\leq E_{2}\leq\cdots are the eigenvalues of HH, the lowest eigenvalue of ℋ\mathcal{H} in this antisymmetric sector is the sum of the lowest KK physical energies. The variational objective is therefore

ℰ=⟨ |ℋ| ⟩⟨ | ⟩≥∑a=1KEa.\mathcal{E}=\frac{\langle\Psi|\mathcal{H}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\geq\sum_{a=1}^{K}E_{a}. (31)

Linearly dependent state functions make the determinant identically zero, excluding collapse onto fewer than KK independent states without pairwise orthogonality penalties.

LaQX samples pNES​(𝒩)=|detM|2/∑𝒩′|detM⁡(𝒩′)|2p_{\mathrm{NES}}(\mathcal{N})=|\det M|^{2}/\sum_{\mathcal{N}^{\prime}}|\det M(\mathcal{N}^{\prime})|^{2}. A Metropolis-Hastings proposal changes one replica and uses the ratio of these determinants in Eq. (17). Define the matrix ℬb​a(𝒩)=(H)a(𝐧b)\mathcal{B}_{ba}(\mathcal{N})=(H{}_{a})(\mathbf{n}_{b}). Acting with H(b)H^{(b)} replaces row bb of MM by the corresponding row of ℬ\mathcal{B}; summing these row replacements gives

𝖤loc​(𝒩)\displaystyle\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{N}) =M−1ℬ,ℰ=⟨Tr𝖤loc⟩pNES,\displaystyle=M^{-1}\mathcal{B},\qquad\mathcal{E}=\left\langle\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{loc}}\right\rangle_{p_{\mathrm{NES}}}, (32)
(ℋ​ )​(𝒩) ⁡(𝒩)\displaystyle\frac{(\mathcal{H}\Psi)(\mathcal{N})}{\Psi(\mathcal{N})} =Tr⁡𝖤loc​(𝒩).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathcal{N}).

Consequently, the same energy-gradient and optimizer formulas apply to log⁡ \log\Psi and the scalar trace. ACE-NES supplies the individual functions using a shared ACE feature extractor and KK state-resolved orbital outputs. Each a is itself a fermionic determinant over occupied orbitals; the additional determinant in Eq. (29) acts on whole many-body states, not on individual particles.

After optimization, the full energy matrix is accumulated rather than only its trace. Let Ga​b=⟨|a⟩bG_{ab}=\langle{}_{a}|{}_{b}\rangle and 𝖧a​b=⟨|aH|⟩b\mathsf{H}_{ab}=\langle{}_{a}|H|{}_{b}\rangle. For linearly independent functions, its exact expectation satisfies [40]

𝖤¯\displaystyle\overline{\mathsf{E}} =⟨𝖤loc⟩pNES=G−1​𝖧,\displaystyle=\langle\mathsf{E}_{\mathrm{loc}}\rangle_{p_{\mathrm{NES}}}=G^{-1}\mathsf{H}, (33)
𝖤¯​ca\displaystyle\overline{\mathsf{E}}\,c_{a} =ℰa​ca⟺𝖧​ca=ℰa​G​ca.\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{a}c_{a}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathsf{H}c_{a}=\mathcal{E}_{a}Gc_{a}.

2.6 Adiabatic evolution

Adiabatic evolution is approximated by a sequence of variational optimizations for nearby Hamiltonians H⁡('j)H(\varphi_{j}), where jj labels successive values of a control parameter '\varphi. Starting from a prepared state, the optimized parameters at 'j\varphi_{j} initialize the calculation at 'j+1\varphi_{j+1}:

�j+1=arg​min�←�j⁡⟨�|H('j+1)|�⟩⟨�|�⟩.\theta_{j+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\leftarrow\theta_{j}}\frac{\langle{}_{\theta}|H(\varphi_{j+1})|{}_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle{}_{\theta}|{}_{\theta}\rangle}. (42)

The arrow denotes initialization at �j\theta_{j}. Small parameter increments and a fixed symmetry sector allow the optimization to follow a continuous low-energy branch.

In the charge-pumping application [13], '\varphi is a boundary twist increased from zero to 2​�2\pi. In the Hofstadter implementation, the xx-direction hopping takes the uniform-gauge form

Hx(')=−∑x,y(ei​'/Lxcx+1,y†cx,y+H.c.).H_{x}(\varphi)=-\sum_{x,y}\left(e^{i\varphi/L_{x}}c_{x+1,y}^{\dagger}c_{x,y}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right). (43)

Thus hopping in the positive xx direction carries ei​'/Lxe^{i\varphi/L_{x}}, and reverse hopping carries its complex conjugate. The accumulated phase around the periodic xx direction is ei​'e^{i\varphi}, so increasing '\varphi by 2​�2\pi inserts one flux quantum through the torus. Each step is followed by a polarization measurement. Continuing the low-energy momentum sectors separately gives the charge-pumping response described in Sec. 4.5.

3 Function-oriented software design

3.1 Composition of the numerical workflow

In LaQX, a complete calculation is divided into four scientific components: the variational state, the Hamiltonian and observables, the sampling procedure, and the parameter-update rule. Each component is exposed through a small functional interface, so a complete workflow is assembled by composition rather than through a hierarchy of stateful solver objects. Numerical state is passed explicitly between components. This design permits compilation, vectorization, automatic differentiation, and device parallelism to be applied to the assembled numerical update [5].

The state layer implements the architectures described in Sec. 2.2, together with the ACE-NES and ACE-PEFT specializations of Secs. 2.4 and 2.7. Independently, the operator layer represents Hamiltonians and observables through the configurations and matrix elements connected to each sampled occupation vector. Sampling and optimization then act on these common representations without depending on the internal construction of a particular ansatz or model.

This separation also determines the parallelization strategy. Batches of sampled configurations are distributed across accelerator devices, while the variational parameters and update state are shared. Ground-state optimization methods reuse the same outer VMC workflow, and measurement, projection, excited-state, and dynamical calculations reuse the same state and operator interfaces. The architecture therefore separates physical definitions from sampling, optimization, and distributed execution while preserving a common numerical core.

3.2 Locality of changes and LLM-assisted development

Small functional interfaces also support LLM-assisted programming. Reconstructing a large inheritance hierarchy or tracing implicit mutable state across many files consumes additional context and tokens, increasing the cost of a change. In LaQX, many extensions require only the relevant scientific component and its interface to be included in the context.

Table 1 summarizes this locality at the level of scientific concepts. A new Hamiltonian defines its connected configurations and matrix elements, after which the existing local-energy and sampling machinery can be reused. A new ansatz supplies initialization and amplitude evaluation without changing the Hamiltonian or optimization methods. Likewise, a new update rule can operate on the common stochastic estimators without depending on the construction of the state.

The example of the altermagnetic Hubbard model in Sec. 4.3 provides a concrete measure of this locality.

4 Physical applications

We now specify the example physical problems used to exercise the code. They cover fermionic and spin ground states, one-body observables, many-body topological responses, low-energy manifolds, and real-time dynamics. Reproducible input specifications and documentation accompany each example in the library.

The square-lattice Hubbard Hamiltonian [29] is defined as

HHub=−t∑⟨i,j⟩,�(ci​�†cj​�+cj​�†ci​�)+U∑ini↑ni↓.H_{\mathrm{Hub}}=-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,\sigma}\left(c_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{j\sigma}+c_{j\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{i\sigma}\right)+U\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}. (49)

Here ci​�†c_{i\sigma}^{\dagger} creates a fermion of spin �\sigma at site ii, ni​�=ci​�†​ci​�n_{i\sigma}=c_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{i\sigma}, ni=ni↑+ni↓n_{i}=n_{i\uparrow}+n_{i\downarrow}, and ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle denotes nearest-neighbor bonds. We set t=1t=1 and consider only nearest-neighbor hopping in this benchmark. Extensions with next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime} are used in studies of competing stripe and superconducting orders [48, 65, 45].

The frustrated spin benchmark uses the square-lattice spin-1/21/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg Hamiltonian

HJ1​J2=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j.H_{J_{1}J_{2}}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}. (50)

The interacting Hofstadter examples [28, 13] use

HHof=−∑x,y(cx+1,y†cx,y+e2​�​i​�​xcx,y+1†cx,y+h.c.)+V∑⟨i,j⟩ninj,H_{\mathrm{Hof}}=-\sum_{x,y}\left(c_{x+1,y}^{\dagger}c_{x,y}+e^{2\pi i\alpha x}c_{x,y+1}^{\dagger}c_{x,y}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)+V\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}n_{i}n_{j}, (51)

The resulting set of calculations is summarized in Table 2.

4.1 Doped Hubbard ground states and GFMC

Large fermionic ansatzes are initialized through a sequence of variational states and Hamiltonians [24, 12]. The reference state is a determinant constructed directly from trainable local orbital embeddings,

M(i,s),jref​(𝐧)\displaystyle M^{\mathrm{ref}}_{(i,s),j}(\mathbf{n}) =Ai,qi,s,j,\displaystyle=A_{i,q_{i},s,j}, (54)
ref(𝐧;A)\displaystyle{}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathbf{n};A) =det[MIa​(𝐧),jref​(𝐧)]a,j=1N.\displaystyle=\det\!\left[M^{\mathrm{ref}}_{I_{a}(\mathbf{n}),j}(\mathbf{n})\right]_{a,j=1}^{N}.

Here qi=ni↑+2​ni↓q_{i}=n_{i\uparrow}+2n_{i\downarrow} labels the local occupation, ss is the spin channel, jj is the orbital index, and Ia​(𝐧)I_{a}(\mathbf{n}) labels the occupied spin orbitals as in Eq. (9). The entries Ai,qi,s,jA_{i,q_{i},s,j} are optimized directly, with no convolutional or MLP layers.

Both Hubbard calculations use 1/81/8 hole doping. For the periodic 16×416\times 4 lattice with N=56N=56 electrons, this reference state is first optimized at U=4U=4 with Adam. It then initializes an ACE state, optimized for 3000030000 MARCH steps at U=8U=8. For the periodic 16×816\times 8 lattice with N=112N=112, the reference stage includes a stripe-pinning field of strength 0.050.05 and charge period eight, targeting a filled stripe [23]. The field is removed for the final 2000020000-step SCALE optimization at U=8U=8. Both optimizations use 40964096 walkers. The ACE state has 12 convolutional layers of width 128; SCALE uses width 256 and four site-wise nonlinear layers of width 512, following the architecture families of Ref. [23].

The local observables in Fig. 2 show the hole density hi=1−⟨ni↑+ni↓⟩h_{i}=1-\langle n_{i\uparrow}+n_{i\downarrow}\rangle through site colors and the spin polarization ⟨Siz⟩=⟨ni↑−ni↓⟩/2\langle S_{i}^{z}\rangle=\langle n_{i\uparrow}-n_{i\downarrow}\rangle/2 through vertical arrows. Both states exhibit filled stripes [69] with a charge-density-wave wavelength of eight sites along the long direction and an antiphase modulation of the staggered magnetization mi=(−1)xi+yi​⟨Siz⟩m_{i}=(-1)^{x_{i}+y_{i}}\langle S_{i}^{z}\rangle.

Evaluation of the final states gives energies per site of −0.762822​(5)-0.762822(5) for ACE on 16×416\times 4 and −0.753059​(7)-0.753059(7) for SCALE on 16×816\times 8. Both states are subsequently used as importance-sampling and fixed-node guiding functions for the GFMC algorithm of Sec. 2.5, with the Hamiltonians and boundary conditions held fixed. Discarding the first 10001000 of 50005000 projection steps gives energies per site of −0.76378​(2)-0.76378(2) for ACE-guided GFMC and −0.75628​(3)-0.75628(3) for SCALE-guided GFMC. These estimates lower the respective VMC energies by approximately 9.6×10−49.6\times 10^{-4} and 3.2×10−33.2\times 10^{-3} per site.

4.2 Frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} spin model

For the spin benchmark we consider the periodic 6×66\times 6 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model defined in Eq. (50) at J1=1J_{1}=1 and J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, in the zero-magnetization sector. The variational state is CNN-MPS with MPS bond dimension D=20D=20 [19]: the convolutional feature map first reorganizes the correlations of the sampled spin configuration, after which a periodic backflow MPS contracts the configuration-dependent tensors as in Eq. (16). The calculation applies the Marshall sign transformation [36] and projection onto the D4D_{4} lattice-symmetry sector. The optimization uses 1500015000 MARCH steps without second-moment accumulator normalization, corresponding to v~k−1=vk−1\widetilde{v}_{k-1}=v_{k-1} in Eq. (25). 4.3 Altermagnetic Hubbard model

The altermagnetic calculation tests both a nonstandard kinetic term and an observable beyond the total energy. The diagonal hopping amplitudes in Eq. (53) are t+=0.4t_{+}=0.4 and t−=0t_{-}=0. A half-filled periodic 12×1212\times 12 system is first optimized at U=3U=3 using the reference determinant ansatz in Eq. (54). This occupation-dependent reference state initializes the subsequent ACE optimization at U=8U=8. The trained state is then sampled to obtain the fermionic one-body density matrix.

Let c𝐤​�=Ns−1/2∑je−i𝐤⋅𝐫jcj​�c_{\mathbf{k}\sigma}=N_{s}^{-1/2}\sum_{j}e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}}c_{j\sigma} annihilate a fermion of momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} and spin �\sigma, where 𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{j} is the position of site jj. The measured momentum distribution is

Figure 4 shows the difference ⟨n𝐤↑⟩−⟨n𝐤↓⟩\langle n_{\mathbf{k}\uparrow}\rangle-\langle n_{\mathbf{k}\downarrow}\rangle, highlighting the anisotropic spin-dependent momentum structure obtained from this estimator.

4.4 Hofstadter low-energy spectrum with NES

The NES calculation uses a 12×412\times 4 interacting Hofstadter system with N=4N=4 spin-polarized particles, �=0.25\alpha=0.25, and V=2V=2. Four state-resolved determinant outputs share the nonlinear ACE feature extractor and are optimized jointly through the auxiliary determinant in Eq. (29), under either open or periodic boundary conditions. Sampling after optimization gives the 4×44\times 4 energy matrix; its Monte Carlo mean is diagonalized to resolve the energies represented in the learned subspace. Figure 5 compares these eigenvalues with ED.

The open-boundary NES energies are approximately −10.5473-10.5473, −10.4485-10.4485, −10.4265-10.4265, and −10.4066-10.4066, with deviations from ED ranging from 4.6×10−54.6\times 10^{-5} to 1.0×10−41.0\times 10^{-4}. The finite cluster has a nondegenerate ground state separated from the first excitation by approximately 0.0990.099.

For periodic boundaries, the energies are approximately −11.1322-11.1322, −11.1295-11.1295, −11.1295-11.1295, and −11.0665-11.0665. The lowest three states form a closely spaced group, while the fourth lies about 0.0630.063 above the third. The first three deviations from ED are below 6.1×10−46.1\times 10^{-4}, whereas the fourth is about 4.5×10−34.5\times 10^{-3}, indicating a less accurate representation of that state. At filling �=N/(�​Ns)=1/3\nu=N/(\alpha N_{s})=1/3, this three-state manifold is consistent with the torus ground-state structure of a fractional quantum Hall phase [13]. Section 4.5 examines the associated fractional charge-pumping response.

4.5 Hofstadter charge pumping

Following the charge-pumping formulation of Ref. [13], Eq. (51) is defined on a periodic 12×812\times 8 lattice with N=8N=8 spin-polarized particles, �=0.25\alpha=0.25, and V=2V=2. In this gauge, the magnetic unit cell spans four sites along xx. The integers Kx=0,1,2K_{x}=0,1,2 and Ky=0,…,7K_{y}=0,\ldots,7 label momentum sectors for translations by one magnetic unit cell along xx and one site along yy, respectively. For a translation by (4​m,n)(4m,n) sites, the symmetry-projection phase is

�Kx,Ky(m,n)=exp[2�i(Kx​m3+Ky​n8)],m=0,1,2,n=0,…,7.\chi_{K_{x},K_{y}}(m,n)=\exp\!\left[2\pi i\left(\frac{K_{x}m}{3}+\frac{K_{y}n}{8}\right)\right],\qquad m=0,1,2,\quad n=0,\ldots,7. (57)

The sector scan identifies three low-energy states at (Kx,Ky)=(0,4)(K_{x},K_{y})=(0,4), (1,4)(1,4), and (2,4)(2,4), as shown in Fig. 6 (left). Their measured total energies are −21.85505​(9)-21.85505(9), −21.84695​(9)-21.84695(9), and −21.84713​(9)-21.84713(9), respectively; the next level in the scanned sectors lies at −21.81715​(8)-21.81715(8), about 0.0300.030 above the top of this manifold. The finite variational splitting within the manifold is approximately 0.00810.0081. Separate adiabatic-continuation calculations follow these three states using the protocol of Sec. 2.6. The boundary twist '\varphi increases from 00 to 2​�2\pi, inserting one flux quantum.

At each flux value, the yy-direction Resta polarization is measured [46],

Z^y=exp⁡(2​�​iLy​∑x,yy​n^x,y),Py​(')=12​�​Im​log⁡⟨Z^y⟩'.\hat{Z}_{y}=\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{L_{y}}\sum_{x,y}y\,\hat{n}_{x,y}\right),\qquad P_{y}(\varphi)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\mathrm{Im}\log\langle\hat{Z}_{y}\rangle_{\varphi}. (58)

The measured phase is unwrapped before division by 2​�2\pi. Separate linear fits of PyP_{y} against '/(2​�)\varphi/(2\pi) give slopes 0.3340.334, 0.3350.335, and 0.3300.330 for the three continued states (Fig. 6, right). Each branch therefore pumps approximately one third of a particle per inserted flux quantum, with a combined response of approximately one particle. This fractional response is consistent with flux insertion connecting states within a topological ground-state manifold [13].

LaQX was also used in a recent study of the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model [25]. There, LaQX-based NQS and independent PEPS calculations provided complementary evidence of spin-charge separation from spin pumping and real-time spin and charge dynamics. This application is distinct from the spin-polarized charge-pumping example documented here, but it demonstrates that the Hofstadter workflows extend to interacting spinful fermions and cross-method validation.

4.6 Real-time tVMC

The real-time calculation considers the density response to the removal of a local potential. An ACE reference state is first optimized for an open 8×68\times 6 Hofstadter lattice with N=4N=4 spin-polarized particles, V=2V=2, �=0.25\alpha=0.25, and the pinning term hv​n0h_{v}n_{0} with hv=−4h_{v}=-4. At t=0t=0, the pinning term is removed and the optimized state initializes the ACE-PEFT evolution.

The ACE-PEFT variant applies Eq. (44): the convolutional and site-wise nonlinear layers of the optimized reference state define a fixed, configuration-dependent neural basis, and only its complex final orbital map evolves. The calculation uses RK4 integration with time step 2×10−32\times 10^{-3}, 4096040960 walkers, and the eigendecomposition solver with smooth cutoff 10−810^{-8}.

The density snapshots and time series in Fig. 7 track the redistribution of the initially pinned charge and reproduce the main features of the ED response.

5 Conclusion

We have introduced LaQX, a JAX implementation of neural quantum state methods for interacting lattice fermions and spins. The code combines Metropolis-Hastings sampling, several variational ansatz families, first-order and natural-gradient optimization, observables, stochastic projection, excited states, adiabatic continuation, and real-time evolution through a common set of functional interfaces. The doped Hubbard and frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model calculations connect the release to methods that have achieved high variational accuracy [24, 23, 19]. The Hofstadter-Hubbard applications encompass many-body charge pumping [13] and NQS calculations of spin-charge separation [25]. The altermagnetic, excited-state, and dynamical examples test the same interfaces on one-body observables, low-energy states, and real-time evolution.

The library separates scientific components through explicit functional interfaces. Wavefunctions, physical operators, and update rules can therefore be extended through local source changes. This locality is useful for conventional development and for LLM-assisted programming, where unnecessary cross-file dependencies consume a finite context window. Source code, documentation, and the scripts used for the calculations in this paper are available at https://github.com/bytedance/laqx.
